newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's military red-faced over security lapse.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's military red-faced over security lapse.

text.p: Embarrassed South Korean naval officers on Wednesday admitted an anti-submarine exercise was under way last month while a North Korean submarine sneaked in unnoticed.
"We held a rather comprehensive exercise between September 15 and 17, including an anti-submarine exercise," said a senior officer.

The Shark-class North Korean vessel ran aground off the eastern city of Kangnung on September 17 as it tried to pick up three spies it offloaded two days earlier, according to the only North Korean captured alive from the vessel.
It lay stuck on rocks unnoticed by security forces until an alert taxi driver spotted the conning tower of the vessel looming out of the darkness the following day.
By then 26 North Koreans involved in the submarine mission had fled to the hills, where 22 have been shot dead. A hunt is under way for three missing intruders.
South Korean news reports said about 10 destroyers, frigates and patrol boats equipped with sonar detectors took part in the exercise near Kangnung.
A navy spokesman declined to give details of the exercise.
The South Korean Defence Ministry, which mobilised 40,000 soldiers to hunt for the North Koreans, said the incursion was preparation for wider military provocation.
Captured North Korean Lee Kwang-soo told reporters on Tuesday his submarine faced little difficulty slipping through South Korean coastal defences.
The incursion rattled South Koreans worried about their safety and led to charges that the military was getting lax and complacent against the North Korean security threat.

Partly to defuse such criticism, and to signal a tougher defence posture, President Kim Young-sam ordered a sweeping reshuffle of the military top brass and sacked his defence minister, Lee Yang-ho, this month.
The ex-minister has since been arrested and charged in an arms procurement bribery scandal.
The captured North Korean, a coxswain, told reporters the submarine passed a South Korean navy vessel equipped with sonar detectors.
"We could evade it with ease," he said.
Asked about South Korean coastal defences against North Korean infilatration, he said: "If you come in by a submarine you can do it as many times as you like."

Seoul has demanded a "clear apology" from Pyongyang over the intrusion, while North Korea has threatened to retaliate "a hundredfold or a thousandfold" over the killings and demanded the return of the bodies, the survivors and the submarine.
